lesson.title: Strings That Span Several Lines
lesson.summary: Triple quotes let a string literal span multiple lines of source code with real line breaks, and are also the standard way to write function docstrings.
lesson.body:
Every string literal you have seen so far in String Basics has lived on a single line of source code, bounded by a pair of single or double quotes. Multiline strings relax that restriction, using triple quotes, either """ or ''', to mark a string literal that can span as many lines of source code as you like, with actual line breaks in your file becoming actual newline characters in the resulting string.

Consider this triple-quoted string:

message = """Dear student,

Your assignment is due Friday.
Please submit it on time.
"""
print(message)

Between the opening triple quote and closing triple quote, everything is taken literally, including the blank line after "Dear student," and the line breaks between each sentence. Tracing through how Python builds this string: it reads "Dear student,", then encounters an actual newline in the source and inserts a \n character, then reads another newline for the blank line, inserting a second \n, then reads "Your assignment is due Friday.", inserts a \n, reads "Please submit it on time.", and inserts a final \n before the closing triple quote. The result is functionally identical to writing the whole message as a single-line string using explicit \n escape characters, connecting directly back to what you learned in Escape Characters. Triple quotes simply let you write it in the more readable, naturally line-broken form instead of typing every \n by hand.

Triple-quoted strings also permit unescaped single and double quotes to appear inside them without any special handling, since the parser is only watching for three consecutive matching quote characters to signal the end, not a single one. This makes them convenient for blocks of text containing dialogue or a mix of quotation styles that would otherwise require careful escaping in a single-quoted or double-quoted string.

A second, very common use for triple-quoted strings has nothing to do with multiline text at all: docstrings, the standard way to document what a function does. Placed as the first statement inside a function body, a triple-quoted string becomes that function's documentation, retrievable later with help():

def area(radius):
    """Return the area of a circle with the given radius."""
    return 3.14159 * radius ** 2

Here the docstring happens to fit on one line, and triple quotes are used purely by convention for docstrings, not because the text spans multiple lines, though a longer docstring explaining parameters and return values in detail would genuinely take advantage of the multiline capability.

One caution worth flagging: because triple-quoted strings preserve exact indentation from your source file, indenting a multiline string to match the surrounding code's indentation level will bake that leading whitespace into the string itself, on every line after the first. Watching for this, or stripping it afterward, matters if the resulting text needs to be clean.
